{{Short description|Professor of Mathematics}}
{{About|the author and recreational mathematician|the German industrialist|Robert Bosch}}

'''Robert A. (Bob) Bosch''' (born August 13, 1963, in [[Buffalo, New York|Buffalo NY]]) is an author, recreational mathematician and the James F. Clark Professor of Mathematics at [[Oberlin College]].<ref name=oberlan>[https://www.oberlin.edu/bob-bosch Robert Bosch at Oberlin College] home page</ref> He is known for domino art<ref name=oberlan_mag>[https://www2.oberlin.edu/alummag/winter2014/thoughtprocess.html Thought Process: Hypothesis Bosch] Oberlin Alumni Magazine Winter 2014] Vol 109 No. 1</ref> and for combining [[graph theory]] and [[mathematical optimization]] to design connect-the-dots eye candy:<ref name=SA_op_art>''[https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/roots-of-unity/the-mathematics-of-opt-art/ The Mathematics of Opt Art]'', Review by Evelyn Lamb, Scientific American, 03 January, 2020</ref> labyrinths, [[knight's tour]]s, [[string art]] and TSP Art.<ref>[https://wiki.evilmadscientist.com/TSP%20art TSP art] Evil Mad Scientist Wiki</ref>

He is the author of ''Opt Art: From Mathematical Optimization to Visual Design''.<ref>''[https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691164069/opt-art Opt Art: From Mathematical Optimization to Visual Design]'' by Robert Bosch, Princeton University Press, (2019), {{ISBN| 9780691164069}}</ref>

==Education and career==
Bosch received a BA in [[mathematics]] at [[Oberlin College]] in 1985, an MS in [[operations research]] and [[statistics]] at [[Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute]] in 1987 and a PhD in operations research where he completed his thesis titled, ''Partial Updating in Interior-Point Methods for Linear Programming'' under Kurt Martin Anstreicher at [[Yale University]] in 1991.<ref name=mgp>[https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=127087 Robert Alexander Mark Boschr] at the [[Mathematics Genealogy Project]]</ref>

He has been at Oberlin College since 1991 where he teaches mathematics, [[statistics]] and [[computer science]].<ref name=oberlan/>

==Combining art and mathematics==
Bosch is passionate about using computers and mathematical optimization techniques to design visual art. He refers to this work as "Opt Art." He has written dozens of papers on this topic, many of them with Oberlin College student collaborators. Over the years, Bosch has created numerous portraits drawn with a single continuous line. Some of these drawings are solutions of the
[[Traveling salesman problem]] (or solutions to related problems). Examples include the "figurative tours" he created with computer scientist Tom Wexler<ref>''[https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/roots-of-unity/when-the-mona-lisa-is-np-hard/ When the Mona Lisa is NP-Hard]'' by Evelyn Lamb, Scientific American, April 31, 2015</ref> and renditions of [[Leonardo da Vinci]]'s [[Mona Lisa|''Mona Lisa'']],<ref>''[https://www.wired.com/2015/06/get-lost-internets-mind-bending-math-inspired-art/ Get Lost in the Internet's Mind-Bending, Math-Inspired Art]'' by Sylvia Chen, [[Wired (magazine)|Wired]], 19 June 2015</ref> [[Vincent van Gogh|Vincent Van Gogh's]] [[self-portrait]], and [[Johannes Vermeer]]'s [[Girl with a Pearl Earring|''Girl with a Pearl Earring'']].<ref>[https://mymodernmet.com/robert-bosch-optimization-art/ Mathematician Creates Intricate Drawings Using One Continuous Line] By Margherita Cole, My Modern Met, February 17</ref>

Domino portraits such as his renderings of [[Martin Luther King]]<ref>[https://www.sfgate.com/education/article/SAN-FRANCISCO-Civil-rights-legend-takes-form-2646819.php Students' MLK mural made of dominoes will have place of honor with 'a lot of George Washingtons] by Jill Tucker, San Francisco Chronicle, 23 February 2007</ref> and [[Barack Obama]]<ref name=SA_op_art/> are an expansion of the mathematical genre of opt art.<ref name=oberlan_mag/>

==Awards==
* 2007 Trevor Evans Award from the [[Mathematical Association of America]] (MAA), for the ''[[Math Horizons]]'' article "Opt Art".<ref>[https://www.maa.org/press/periodicals/math-horizons/trevor-evans-award-winners Robert Bosch, "Opt Art," Math Horizons, February 2006, pp. 6-9.] Trevor Evans Award Winners</ref>
* 2012 Inaugural Outstanding Paper Award from the [[Journal of Mathematics and the Arts]], for the article "Simple-Close-Curve Sculptures of Knots and Links".<ref>[http://www.dominoartwork.com/about.html Domino Artwork: The Mathematical Artwork of Robert Bosch]</ref>
* 2010 First Prize in the Mathematical Art Exhibition of The [[American Mathematical Society]] (AMS), for the sculpture ''Embrace''.<ref>[https://www.ams.org/publicoutreach/math-imagery/2010-Exhibition 2010 Mathematical Art Exhibition] AMS</ref>
